question: A Lambda function processes payment events. After successful processing, the developer wants to automatically notify a downstream service. If processing fails after all retries, the event should go to a separate SQS queue for manual review. Which Lambda feature handles both success and failure destinations without changing the function code?
choices: Configure the SQS queue as the Lambda event source and use DLQ
Configure Lambda Destinations with an OnSuccess target (EventBridge) and OnFailure target (SQS)
Use a Step Functions state machine to handle success and failure routing
Add try/catch in the function to publish to EventBridge or SQS directly
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure Lambda Destinations with an OnSuccess target (EventBridge) and OnFailure target (SQS)

Lambda Destinations allow you to route asynchronous invocation results without code changes. OnSuccess sends the event payload and function result to a target (EventBridge, SQS, SNS, or another Lambda). OnFailure sends the event payload and error details to a target after all retries are exhausted. This is the recommended approach for async event routing. DLQs only handle failures. Step Functions adds orchestration overhead. Try/catch in code requires code changes and adds complexity.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html#invocation-async-destinations

question: A developer enables DynamoDB Streams on a table. A Lambda function processes stream records to update a search index. The developer needs to ensure that stream records are processed in the order they were written per item. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: Set the Lambda event source mapping batch size to 1
Configure DynamoDB Streams with KEYS_ONLY stream view type
DynamoDB Streams inherently delivers records in order per partition key; ensure the Lambda function does not process batches from the same shard in parallel
Enable DynamoDB global tables to replicate stream ordering across regions
explanation_html:
Correct answer: DynamoDB Streams inherently delivers records in order per partition key; ensure the Lambda function does not process batches from the same shard in parallel

DynamoDB Streams guarantee ordering of records within a shard, and items with the same partition key always go to the same shard. Lambda processes shards sequentially by default (one Lambda invocation per shard at a time), preserving order. To maintain order, the Lambda function should complete processing of each batch before the next is processed for the same shard. Batch size 1 reduces throughput unnecessarily. KEYS_ONLY controls what data is in the record, not ordering. Global tables are for multi-region replication.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html

question: A developer needs to choose between Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon SQS for a use case requiring ordered processing of clickstream events, the ability to reprocess data from 48 hours ago, and support for 5 different consumer applications reading independently. Which service is the best fit and why?
choices: SQS FIFO queue — it guarantees ordering and supports multiple consumers
SQS Standard queue — it offers the highest throughput for multiple consumers
Kinesis Data Streams — it supports ordered records per shard, data retention up to 365 days, and multiple independent consumers via enhanced fan-out
SNS with SQS fanout — it delivers to multiple queues and supports replay
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Kinesis Data Streams — it supports ordered records per shard, data retention up to 365 days, and multiple independent consumers via enhanced fan-out

Kinesis Data Streams provides: ordered records per shard (can route by partition key), configurable retention (24 hours default, up to 365 days), and multiple independent consumers that each maintain their own position in the stream. Enhanced fan-out provides dedicated 2 MB/s bandwidth per consumer per shard. SQS FIFO guarantees ordering but once a message is consumed it is deleted — no replay. SQS Standard has no ordering or replay. SNS/SQS fan-out does not support replay.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/introduction.html

question: A developer needs to filter SNS messages so that an SQS queue only receives messages where the attribute 'eventType' equals 'ORDER_PLACED'. How is this implemented?
choices: Configure a CloudWatch Events rule to filter SNS messages before delivery to SQS
Set a subscription filter policy on the SNS subscription for the SQS queue
Add a message attribute filter in the SQS receive message call
Use a Lambda function between SNS and SQS to discard unwanted messages
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Set a subscription filter policy on the SNS subscription for the SQS queue

SNS subscription filter policies allow SNS to evaluate message attributes and only deliver messages that match the specified criteria to a particular subscriber. This is done at the SNS level, reducing costs by not delivering irrelevant messages to SQS. The filter policy is a JSON object specifying attribute conditions. CloudWatch Events processes AWS service events, not SNS message routing. SQS does not filter messages at receive time. A Lambda intermediary adds latency and cost unnecessarily.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-message-filtering.html

question: A developer is designing a Step Functions state machine for an order processing workflow. The workflow needs to run tasks in parallel (validate inventory, charge payment, check fraud) and only proceed when all three complete successfully. Which Step Functions state type is appropriate?
choices: Choice state with three branches
Map state iterating over an array of tasks
Parallel state with three branches
Task state with three activity workers
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Parallel state with three branches

The Parallel state executes multiple branches simultaneously and waits for all branches to complete before moving to the next state. Each branch is an independent workflow. If any branch fails, the entire Parallel state fails. This matches the requirement of running three tasks concurrently and proceeding only when all succeed. Choice states implement conditional branching (like switch/if-else). Map states iterate over an array of items. Task states invoke a single resource (Lambda, Activity, etc.).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/amazon-states-language-parallel-state.html

question: A developer needs to atomically transfer $100 from Account A to Account B in DynamoDB. Both the debit from Account A and the credit to Account B must either both succeed or both fail. Which DynamoDB feature supports this?
choices: DynamoDB conditional expressions on each UpdateItem call
DynamoDB transactions using TransactWriteItems
DynamoDB batch write using BatchWriteItem
DynamoDB optimistic locking with version attributes on both items
explanation_html:
Correct answer: DynamoDB transactions using TransactWriteItems

DynamoDB transactions provide ACID guarantees for up to 100 items across multiple tables. TransactWriteItems performs all operations atomically — either all succeed or all fail with no partial updates. This is the correct choice for financial transfers requiring both-or-nothing semantics. Conditional expressions on separate UpdateItem calls are not atomic — the second call could fail after the first succeeds, leaving inconsistent state. BatchWriteItem is not atomic; it has no all-or-nothing guarantee. Optimistic locking with versioning helps detect conflicts but does not provide atomicity across multiple items.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/transactions.html

question: A developer wants to run lightweight JavaScript at CloudFront edge locations to modify HTTP request and response headers. The function must execute in under 1ms and does not need network access or file system access. Which option is most appropriate?
choices: Lambda@Edge with a viewer request trigger
CloudFront Functions with a viewer request event
API Gateway Lambda authorizer at the edge
CloudFront origin request Lambda@Edge
explanation_html:
Correct answer: CloudFront Functions with a viewer request event

CloudFront Functions are lightweight JavaScript functions that execute at CloudFront edge locations with sub-millisecond latency. They are ideal for simple header manipulation, URL rewriting, and request/response transformation. They have stricter limits (no network access, no file system, 1ms compute time, 10 KB package size) but are significantly cheaper and faster than Lambda@Edge. Lambda@Edge supports Node.js and Python with up to 5 seconds execution time and network/file system access — appropriate for more complex logic but overkill for simple header manipulation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cloudfront-functions.html

question: A Kinesis Data Stream has 4 shards. Each shard can handle 1,000 records/second for writes. The application is producing 5,000 records/second and experiencing throttling. What is the most direct solution?
choices: Enable Kinesis enhanced fan-out to increase write throughput
Use the Kinesis PutRecords API instead of PutRecord to batch writes
Increase the number of shards in the stream to at least 5
Enable Kinesis Data Streams on-demand mode
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Increase the number of shards in the stream to at least 5

Each Kinesis shard supports 1,000 records/second (1 MB/s) for writes and 2 MB/s for reads. With 4 shards the maximum write throughput is 4,000 records/second. To handle 5,000 records/second, at least 5 shards are needed. You can reshard using the UpdateShardCount API. Enhanced fan-out increases read throughput per consumer, not write throughput. PutRecords batches multiple records in one API call (reducing API overhead) but does not increase the shard-level throughput limit. On-demand mode scales automatically but the question asks for the most direct solution to a known throughput deficit.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/service-sizes-and-limits.html

question: A developer is building a multi-tenant SaaS application. Each tenant's data must be stored in the same DynamoDB table but completely isolated. Which approach provides strong tenant isolation at the data layer without over-provisioning tables?
choices: Create a separate DynamoDB table per tenant
Use tenantId as the partition key, and enforce IAM condition keys (dynamodb:LeadingKeys) in tenant-scoped roles
Encrypt each tenant's data with a different KMS key and store them in the same table
Use DynamoDB conditional expressions to filter by tenantId on every query
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use tenantId as the partition key, and enforce IAM condition keys (dynamodb:LeadingKeys) in tenant-scoped roles

The dynamodb:LeadingKeys IAM condition key restricts a principal's DynamoDB access to items where the partition key matches a specific value. Combined with using tenantId as the partition key, each tenant's role can only access their own partition, providing strong data isolation without separate tables. Separate tables per tenant create management overhead and waste provisioned capacity. KMS per-tenant encryption adds privacy but not access isolation (a tenant could still query another tenant's encrypted items). Application-level filtering with conditional expressions is not enforced at the IAM layer and can be bypassed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/specifying-conditions.html

question: A developer needs a DynamoDB table to be accessible with low latency from both us-east-1 and eu-west-1 regions. Writes in either region should be reflected in both regions within seconds. Which DynamoDB feature provides this?
choices: DynamoDB cross-region replication using DynamoDB Streams and Lambda
DynamoDB Global Tables
DynamoDB DAX clusters deployed in both regions
DynamoDB point-in-time recovery with cross-region restore
explanation_html:
Correct answer: DynamoDB Global Tables

DynamoDB Global Tables provide fully managed, multi-region, multi-active replication. You can read and write to the table in any replica region, and changes propagate to all other regions within seconds. It handles conflict resolution automatically using last-writer-wins semantics. Custom Streams+Lambda replication adds operational complexity and is harder to keep consistent. DAX is an in-memory cache that reduces read latency but does not replicate data across regions. PITR is for point-in-time backup and recovery, not active multi-region access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html

question: A developer creates a Lambda function URL to expose a function as an HTTPS endpoint. The function must only be accessible to requests that include a valid JWT in the Authorization header. Which auth type should be configured on the function URL?
choices: AWS_IAM — requires Signature Version 4 signed requests
NONE with a Lambda authorizer attached
COGNITO with a user pool configured
AWS_IAM is the only option; JWT validation must be implemented inside the function code
explanation_html:
Correct answer: AWS_IAM — requires Signature Version 4 signed requests

Lambda Function URLs support two auth types: AWS_IAM (requires SigV4 signed requests, authorizes based on IAM policies) and NONE (no built-in auth). There is no native JWT/Cognito auth type for function URLs. For JWT validation, the developer should set the auth type to NONE and validate the JWT inside the function code, or place API Gateway in front of the function URL and use a Cognito or Lambda authorizer on API Gateway. If AWS_IAM is chosen, callers must sign requests with SigV4 using valid AWS credentials.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/urls-auth.html

question: A developer notices that messages in an SQS queue are being received and deleted by the consumer but the same messages are appearing again after a few minutes. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SQS queue has duplicate message detection enabled
The consumer is calling ReceiveMessage but not calling DeleteMessage after processing
The visibility timeout has expired before processing completed and DeleteMessage was called
Another consumer in a different thread is receiving the same messages
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The consumer is calling ReceiveMessage but not calling DeleteMessage after processing

In SQS, receiving a message does not automatically delete it. The consumer must explicitly call DeleteMessage using the receipt handle after successful processing. If DeleteMessage is not called, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout expires and can be received by any consumer. This is by design — it ensures at-least-once delivery. Duplicate detection (ContentBasedDeduplication) is a FIFO feature that prevents sending duplicates, not receiving them. Visibility timeout expiry would also cause re-appearance but the question states messages are being 'deleted' — implying DeleteMessage is being called.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-message-lifecycle.html

question: A developer is using AWS AppSync to build a GraphQL API. They need a resolver that queries a DynamoDB table and returns items matching a filter. Which AppSync resolver type directly connects to DynamoDB without requiring a Lambda function?
choices: A Lambda resolver with a DynamoDB SDK call inside
A direct Lambda resolver using the AppSync Lambda data source
A VTL (Velocity Template Language) resolver using the DynamoDB data source
An HTTP resolver pointing to the DynamoDB API endpoint
explanation_html:
Correct answer: A VTL (Velocity Template Language) resolver using the DynamoDB data source

AppSync supports direct integrations with DynamoDB, Lambda, RDS, OpenSearch, and HTTP APIs as data sources. Using the DynamoDB data source with VTL request and response mapping templates, AppSync can directly query DynamoDB without a Lambda intermediary. This reduces latency and cost. AppSync also supports JavaScript resolvers (pipeline resolvers) for DynamoDB. Lambda resolvers add a function invocation overhead. HTTP resolvers pointing to DynamoDB would require constructing raw DynamoDB API requests, which is impractical.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appsync/latest/devguide/tutorial-dynamodb-resolvers.html

question: A DynamoDB table serves a read-heavy application with a frequently accessed hot key (a popular product ID). Read operations on this key are being throttled despite sufficient provisioned capacity on the table. What is the recommended solution?
choices: Enable DynamoDB auto scaling to add capacity dynamically
Use DynamoDB DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) to cache frequently read items
Switch to DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode
Add a random suffix to the partition key to distribute hot key reads
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use DynamoDB DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) to cache frequently read items

DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB that provides microsecond read latency and reduces read load on DynamoDB by caching items. For hot keys that are read frequently, DAX serves subsequent reads from cache without hitting DynamoDB, eliminating throttling. DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB — minimal code changes required. Auto scaling adjusts capacity but still throttles bursts on hot keys since capacity is distributed evenly across partitions. On-demand mode handles unpredictable traffic but hot key throttling occurs at the partition level regardless of capacity mode. Adding random suffixes is a write scatter technique, not a read optimization.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.html

question: A developer needs to continuously load streaming data from Kinesis Data Streams into Amazon S3 in Parquet format, partitioned by date. Which service handles this transformation and delivery with minimal code?
choices: AWS Lambda with a Kinesis trigger that writes to S3
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with S3 as the destination and Parquet conversion enabled
AWS Glue streaming ETL job consuming from Kinesis
Amazon EMR with a Spark Structured Streaming job
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with S3 as the destination and Parquet conversion enabled

Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed service that loads streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and other destinations. It supports record format conversion (JSON to Parquet/ORC) using a Glue Data Catalog schema, dynamic partitioning by date or other fields, buffering, compression, and encryption — all without writing code. Lambda would require custom code for batching, Parquet conversion, and partitioning. Glue streaming ETL and EMR are more complex and expensive for this use case.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/dynamic-partitioning.html

question: A developer deploys a Lambda function as a container image. The image is 800 MB. The developer notices very long cold start times of over 10 seconds. What is the most effective way to reduce container image cold start time?
choices: Move the function code to a ZIP deployment package instead of a container
Enable Lambda SnapStart for the function
Configure provisioned concurrency to keep execution environments warm
Reduce the container image size by using a minimal base image and multi-stage builds
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure provisioned concurrency to keep execution environments warm

Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments, keeping them ready to respond immediately. This eliminates cold starts entirely for the provisioned instances, regardless of image size. Lambda SnapStart is only available for Java runtimes and snapshots the initialized execution environment. While reducing image size and using ZIP packages also reduce cold start time, provisioned concurrency is the most effective solution for eliminating cold starts when latency is critical. Reducing image size is a good practice but may not be sufficient for sub-second cold starts with large images.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html

question: A developer creates an AWS SAM template to define an API Gateway and Lambda function. They want to test the API locally before deploying to AWS. Which command runs the API locally using SAM?
choices: sam build && sam package
sam local start-api
sam deploy --guided --local
sam invoke --local-api
explanation_html:
Correct answer: sam local start-api

The sam local start-api command starts a local HTTP server that hosts all functions defined with API event sources in the SAM template. It emulates API Gateway and invokes Lambda functions in Docker containers locally. sam build compiles and prepares the application for deployment. sam package uploads artifacts to S3 for deployment. sam deploy deploys to AWS. There is no sam invoke --local-api command.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/serverless-application-model/latest/developerguide/sam-cli-command-reference-sam-local-start-api.html

question: A developer needs to use AWS Secrets Manager to store and retrieve secrets in a Lambda function. The function is invoked thousands of times per second. Calling GetSecretValue on every invocation would hit the Secrets Manager API rate limit. What is the recommended caching strategy?
choices: Store the secret in a Lambda environment variable and update it manually when rotated
Use the AWS Secrets Manager caching client library (available for Java, Python, .NET) to cache secrets locally in the Lambda execution environment
Store the secret in ElastiCache and have Lambda read from the cache
Retrieve the secret once per day using a scheduled Lambda and store it in SSM Parameter Store
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use the AWS Secrets Manager caching client library (available for Java, Python, .NET) to cache secrets locally in the Lambda execution environment

AWS provides Secrets Manager caching client libraries that cache secrets in memory within the Lambda execution environment. The cache is refreshed periodically (default: 1 hour) or when a secret fails validation (to handle rotation). This dramatically reduces Secrets Manager API calls while still getting updated secrets after rotation. Lambda environment variables do not update automatically on rotation. ElastiCache adds infrastructure and VPC complexity. A daily refresh via SSM is not responsive enough for rotation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/retrieving-secrets_cache.html

question: A DynamoDB table is in provisioned capacity mode with 100 WCUs. A batch job writes 500 items (each 1 KB) in a 1-second burst. What happens?
choices: All 500 writes succeed because DynamoDB auto-scales during the burst
DynamoDB throttles writes exceeding 100 WCU/s; excess write requests receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException
DynamoDB queues the excess writes and processes them when capacity is available
DynamoDB automatically switches to on-demand mode to handle the burst
explanation_html:
Correct answer: DynamoDB throttles writes exceeding 100 WCU/s; excess write requests receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException

In provisioned capacity mode, DynamoDB provides exactly the provisioned capacity and throttles requests that exceed it with a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Each 1 KB write consumes 1 WCU. Writing 500 × 1 KB items requires 500 WCUs but only 100 are provisioned. DynamoDB does have burst capacity (unused capacity saved for up to 5 minutes) but it is not guaranteed. Auto Scaling adjusts capacity but cannot react to instant bursts. DynamoDB does not queue excess writes or automatically switch modes.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/ProvisionedThroughput.html

question: A developer builds an API Gateway REST API that must accept a request body in a specific JSON schema. Invalid requests should be rejected at API Gateway without invoking the Lambda backend. Which API Gateway feature handles this?
choices: API Gateway usage plans with request validation
API Gateway request validators with a model schema
AWS WAF rules attached to the API Gateway stage
A Lambda authorizer that validates the request body
explanation_html:
Correct answer: API Gateway request validators with a model schema

API Gateway request validators validate request parameters and body against a configured model (JSON Schema). You define a model for the request body and associate a request validator with the method. If the request doesn't match the schema, API Gateway returns a 400 Bad Request without invoking the backend Lambda. This reduces cost and latency by rejecting invalid requests early. Usage plans throttle requests per client but do not validate request content. WAF provides security rules (SQL injection, XSS) but not schema validation. Lambda authorizers can validate the body but still invoke a Lambda function for each request.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-method-request-validation.html

question: A developer is building a real-time chat application using API Gateway WebSocket APIs. When a user sends a message, the Lambda backend needs to push the message to all connected users. How does the Lambda function send messages to other connected WebSocket clients?
choices: Lambda publishes to an SNS topic that each client subscribes to
Lambda calls the API Gateway Management API's PostToConnection endpoint with the connection ID of each recipient
Lambda uses a WebSocket client to re-connect and broadcast the message
Lambda triggers API Gateway to resend the message to all active connections automatically
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Lambda calls the API Gateway Management API's PostToConnection endpoint with the connection ID of each recipient

API Gateway WebSocket APIs maintain persistent connections identified by a connectionId. When a Lambda function needs to send a message to a connected client, it calls the API Gateway Management API's @connections endpoint: POST /{connectionId}. The function retrieves all active connection IDs from a store (e.g., DynamoDB) and sends messages to each one. SNS does not maintain WebSocket connections. Lambda cannot re-connect as a WebSocket client to API Gateway. API Gateway does not automatically broadcast messages to all connections.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-how-to-call-websocket-api-connections.html

question: A developer uses SSM Parameter Store to store a database password as a SecureString. The Lambda function reading the parameter is getting an AccessDeniedException. What permissions does the Lambda execution role need?
choices: ssm:GetParameter and the SSM service role
ssm:GetParameter on the parameter ARN and kms:Decrypt on the KMS key used to encrypt it
ssm:GetParameter and ssm:DescribeParameters on the parameter
kms:GenerateDataKey and ssm:PutParameter
explanation_html:
Correct answer: ssm:GetParameter on the parameter ARN and kms:Decrypt on the KMS key used to encrypt it

SecureString parameters in SSM are encrypted with a KMS key. To retrieve and decrypt a SecureString, the caller needs both ssm:GetParameter (to retrieve the encrypted value from SSM) and kms:Decrypt (to decrypt it using the KMS key). If only ssm:GetParameter is granted, the parameter is returned in encrypted form and cannot be used. ssm:DescribeParameters retrieves metadata, not values. kms:GenerateDataKey is for encryption, not decryption. ssm:PutParameter is for writing parameters.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/sysman-paramstore-access.html

question: A developer needs to implement Cognito User Pool advanced security features to detect and respond to anomalous login behavior (e.g., impossible travel, compromised credentials). Which Cognito feature provides this?
choices: Cognito User Pool MFA with TOTP
Cognito User Pool adaptive authentication (compromised credentials detection and account takeover protection)
Cognito User Pool Lambda trigger for custom authentication flow
Cognito Identity Pool with enhanced risk-based access
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Cognito User Pool adaptive authentication (compromised credentials detection and account takeover protection)

Cognito Advanced Security Features include: Compromised Credentials Detection (checks against known breached password lists), and Account Takeover Protection (detects anomalous sign-in activity like impossible travel and device changes, then can block, MFA-challenge, or allow based on risk level). These features are enabled in the User Pool's Advanced Security settings. MFA adds a second factor but doesn't detect anomalies. Custom auth flows require writing your own risk logic. Cognito Identity Pools manage AWS credential vending, not authentication risk.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pool-settings-advanced-security.html

question: A developer is building a multi-region application and needs to use the same KMS key to encrypt data in us-east-1 and decrypt it in eu-west-1 without copying encrypted data between regions. Which KMS feature supports this?
choices: KMS key replication by exporting the key material
KMS multi-region keys
KMS cross-account key sharing with a key policy
KMS grants to allow cross-region decryption
explanation_html:
Correct answer: KMS multi-region keys

KMS multi-region keys are a set of interoperable KMS keys in different regions that share the same key material and key ID. Data encrypted in one region can be decrypted in another region using the related multi-region key, without re-encryption or cross-region API calls. This enables use cases like global DynamoDB tables with client-side encryption. Exporting key material requires importing it as a different key — it would have a different key ID. Cross-account sharing makes a single-region key accessible from another account, not another region. Grants delegate key usage but do not enable cross-region decryption.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/multi-region-keys-overview.html

question: A developer creates an IAM policy for a Lambda execution role. The policy grants s3:PutObject on a specific bucket. When the Lambda function runs, the put operation fails with 'Access Denied'. The role has no permission boundary. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Lambda functions cannot have IAM roles for S3 access
The S3 bucket policy has an explicit Deny for the Lambda execution role
IAM policies on Lambda execution roles do not apply to S3 operations
The Lambda function needs s3:GetObject permission to also write objects
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The S3 bucket policy has an explicit Deny for the Lambda execution role

IAM policy evaluation combines identity-based policies and resource-based policies. An explicit Deny in any policy always wins over an Allow. If the S3 bucket policy explicitly denies the Lambda execution role (or denies all principals except specific ones), the Lambda function will receive Access Denied even though the identity-based policy grants the permission. Lambda execution roles work normally with S3. IAM policies on Lambda roles fully apply to all AWS API calls. s3:PutObject is sufficient for writing; s3:GetObject is for reading.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

question: A developer needs to rotate a database password in Secrets Manager automatically every 30 days. The rotation must update the password in the database and in Secrets Manager atomically. Which component performs the actual rotation logic?
choices: An EventBridge scheduled rule that updates the secret and the database
A Lambda function configured as the rotation function in Secrets Manager
Secrets Manager's built-in rotation engine (no Lambda needed)
An RDS native rotation feature that updates Secrets Manager directly
explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Lambda function configured as the rotation function in Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager invokes a Lambda function to perform the actual rotation. The Lambda function must implement four steps: createSecret (generate new credentials), setSecret (update credentials in the database), testSecret (verify the new credentials work), and finishSecret (mark the new version as current). For some databases (RDS, Redshift, DocumentDB), AWS provides pre-built rotation Lambda functions. You provide or reference one of these functions as the rotation Lambda in the secret's rotation configuration. EventBridge alone cannot atomically update both the database and the secret. RDS does not natively update Secrets Manager.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotating-secrets.html

question: A developer is using Cognito User Pools. Users belong to different groups (admin, user, viewer) that map to different IAM roles. How does the application determine which group a user belongs to after authentication?
choices: The application queries DynamoDB for the user's group membership
The group memberships are included as cognito:groups claims in the ID token
The Cognito User Pool sends a separate API response with the user's groups
The access token's scope field contains the group names
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The group memberships are included as cognito:groups claims in the ID token

When a user belongs to one or more Cognito User Pool groups, those group names are included as the cognito:groups claim in the ID token (JWT). The application can decode the ID token and read the cognito:groups claim to determine group membership. The ID token also contains cognito:preferred_role and cognito:roles claims for role mapping. The access token contains scopes and is used for API authorization. DynamoDB is not involved in standard Cognito group claims. Cognito does not send a separate response for groups.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-settings-attributes.html

question: A developer is defining a CodePipeline that has a Source (CodeCommit), Build (CodeBuild), and Deploy (CodeDeploy) stage. The pipeline must trigger automatically when code is pushed to the main branch. What is the recommended way to configure this trigger?
choices: Configure a CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) rule that matches CodeCommit push events on the main branch and triggers the pipeline
Enable periodic polling in the CodePipeline source stage with a 1-minute interval
Use a CodeCommit repository trigger that directly invokes CodePipeline
Configure a webhook in the CodePipeline source stage
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure a CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) rule that matches CodeCommit push events on the main branch and triggers the pipeline

The recommended approach for triggering CodePipeline from CodeCommit is using an EventBridge rule. When code is pushed to CodeCommit, it emits an event. An EventBridge rule with a source filter for the specific repository and branch triggers the pipeline via the StartPipelineExecution API. This is event-driven and near real-time. Polling introduces latency (up to 1 minute) and is not recommended. CodeCommit repository triggers can invoke Lambda or SNS but do not directly start CodePipeline. Webhooks are used for GitHub/Bitbucket integrations, not CodeCommit.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/pipelines-trigger-source-repo-changes-console.html

question: A developer is configuring CodeBuild to build a project. The buildspec.yml defines install, build, and post_build phases. In which phase should unit tests be run to ensure failed tests abort the build and report the failure?
choices: install phase — before the application is compiled
build phase — tests run alongside compilation and fail the build if they fail
post_build phase — tests run after the build regardless of build outcome
A separate test phase defined after the build phase
explanation_html:
Correct answer: build phase — tests run alongside compilation and fail the build if they fail

In CodeBuild, each phase runs sequentially. If a command in a phase exits with a non-zero code, that phase fails and subsequent phases do not run (unless explicitly configured). Running unit tests in the build phase ensures that if tests fail, the build fails and the post_build phase (which might package artifacts) does not run. The post_build phase runs after the build — it executes even if the build phase fails, making it unsuitable for tests that should block packaging. The install phase is for installing dependencies. CodeBuild does not have a separate named test phase (though test reports can be collected in any phase).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html

question: A developer needs to deploy an application to Amazon ECS using Fargate. The task definition requires a secret (database password) to be available as an environment variable in the container. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Hardcode the password in the ECS task definition environment variables
Store the password in Secrets Manager and reference the secret ARN in the task definition's secrets field
Pass the password as a Docker build argument in the container image
Mount the password from an S3 bucket using a bind mount in the task definition
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Store the password in Secrets Manager and reference the secret ARN in the task definition's secrets field

ECS task definitions support injecting secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store as environment variables at container startup. You specify the secret ARN in the secrets field of the container definition, and ECS retrieves and injects the secret value. The ECS task role must have secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission. This keeps secrets out of the task definition and enables rotation. Hardcoding credentials is a security anti-pattern. Docker build arguments are baked into the image, making rotation impossible. S3 bind mounts are not natively supported in Fargate.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/secrets-envvar-secrets-manager.html

question: A developer needs to use AWS CloudFormation to create an RDS instance. The instance must not be replaced when the MasterUserPassword property changes. Which attribute should be set on the RDS resource?
choices: DeletionPolicy: Retain
UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
UpdatePolicy: NoInterruption
UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot
explanation_html:
Correct answer: UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot

UpdateReplacePolicy specifies the action CloudFormation takes when a resource must be replaced during a stack update. Setting it to Snapshot creates a snapshot of the resource before replacing it — for RDS, this means a DB snapshot is taken before deletion. This protects data in case a property change forces replacement. Retain keeps the old resource without deleting it. DeletionPolicy applies when the stack is deleted. There is no UpdatePolicy: NoInterruption attribute; NoInterruption is a property of the update behavior, not a CloudFormation attribute name.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-attribute-updatereplacepolicy.html

question: A developer is using AWS X-Ray to trace a distributed application. They want to add custom context data to a trace segment that will be available for detailed inspection but does NOT need to be searchable in the X-Ray console. Which X-Ray feature should be used?
choices: X-Ray annotations — indexed key-value pairs for filtering
X-Ray metadata — non-indexed data attached to segments
X-Ray trace groups — saved filter expressions
X-Ray sampling rules — rule-based trace selection
explanation_html:
Correct answer: X-Ray metadata — non-indexed data attached to segments

X-Ray metadata allows attaching arbitrary data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers) to a segment or subsegment for detailed debugging. Unlike annotations, metadata is NOT indexed and cannot be used in filter expressions in the X-Ray console. Metadata is visible when inspecting individual trace details. Use annotations when you need to search/filter traces by a value. Use metadata for large or complex data that is only useful when viewing a specific trace. Trace groups are saved filter expressions. Sampling rules control which requests are traced.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-sdk-nodejs-segment.html

question: A developer needs to configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers when the 95th percentile latency of an API Gateway stage exceeds 2000ms for 5 consecutive minutes. Which CloudWatch statistic should be used in the alarm?
choices: Average
Maximum
Sum
explanation_html:
Correct answer: p95

CloudWatch supports percentile statistics (p0.0 to p100) for metrics collected from multiple data points. p95 represents the 95th percentile — 95% of requests complete faster than this value. Using p95 for a latency alarm is more meaningful than Average (which can be skewed by fast requests) and more actionable than Maximum (which may represent rare outliers). API Gateway's Latency metric supports percentile statistics. Sum of latency is not meaningful for threshold-based alarms.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Statistics-definitions.html

question: A developer builds a CloudFormation custom resource that calls an external API to provision infrastructure not supported by CloudFormation. The custom resource Lambda function must signal success or failure back to CloudFormation. How does the Lambda function signal completion?
choices: Return a success/failure response from the Lambda handler function
Send an HTTP PUT request with a JSON response to the pre-signed S3 URL provided in the event's ResponseURL property
Call the CloudFormation SignalResource API with the stack ID and logical resource ID
Publish to the CloudFormation SNS topic with the stack ARN and status
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Send an HTTP PUT request with a JSON response to the pre-signed S3 URL provided in the event's ResponseURL property

CloudFormation custom resources work by passing a ResponseURL (a pre-signed S3 URL) to the Lambda function in the event. The function must PUT a JSON response to this URL containing Status (SUCCESS or FAILED), StackId, RequestId, LogicalResourceId, and optionally Data (output key-value pairs). CloudFormation polls for this response. If the function fails without sending a response, the stack will wait for the timeout period (1 hour by default). Simply returning from the Lambda handler does not signal CloudFormation. CloudFormation::SignalResource is used for cfn-signal in EC2 user data, not custom resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/crpg-ref-responses.html

question: A developer is building a Lambda function that processes images uploaded to S3. The function uses the Pillow library (a large Python package). They notice deployment package size exceeds Lambda's 50 MB (zipped) limit. What are two valid approaches to solve this? (Select TWO)
choices: Deploy the function as a container image (up to 10 GB)
Include only the required modules from Pillow by tree-shaking the package
Use a Lambda layer for Pillow and keep the function code small
Enable Lambda code compression to reduce the deployment package size
Store Pillow in S3 and download it on each cold start
explanation_html:
Correct answers: Deploy the function as a container image AND Use a Lambda layer for Pillow

When a ZIP deployment package exceeds Lambda's size limits (50 MB zipped, 250 MB unzipped), two recommended approaches are: (1) Container images — Lambda supports container images up to 10 GB, which can include large dependencies. (2) Lambda layers — move large dependencies (like Pillow) to a layer; the layer's size counts toward the total 250 MB unzipped limit but is separate from the function code package. Pillow cannot be tree-shaken as it is a compiled C extension. Lambda does not have a code compression feature beyond standard ZIP. Downloading from S3 on cold start adds latency and unreliability.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html

question: A Step Functions state machine executes a Lambda function. The Lambda function raises a custom error called OrderFulfillmentError. The state machine must catch this specific error and transition to a HandleFulfillmentError state. How is this configured?
choices: Add a Try/Catch block in the Lambda function code to catch the error and invoke Step Functions
Add a Catch field to the Task state with ErrorEquals containing 'OrderFulfillmentError' and Next pointing to HandleFulfillmentError
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda function error metric that triggers a Step Functions execution
Add a Retry field with ErrorEquals containing 'OrderFulfillmentError' and BackoffRate of 0
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Add a Catch field to the Task state with ErrorEquals containing 'OrderFulfillmentError' and Next pointing to HandleFulfillmentError

Step Functions Task states support a Catch field that specifies error handlers. Each catcher has ErrorEquals (list of error names to catch), Next (state to transition to on match), and optionally ResultPath (where to put the error details in the state input). The Lambda function throws the error as a named exception (e.g., raise Exception('OrderFulfillmentError')) and Step Functions catches it by matching the error name. Lambda-side try/catch would prevent Step Functions from seeing the error. CloudWatch alarms operate asynchronously. Retry with BackoffRate 0 would retry without backoff, not transition to an error handler.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html

question: A developer uses Elastic Beanstalk and needs to run a background task (data aggregation) that reads from an SQS queue. The web tier and worker tier should scale independently. Which Elastic Beanstalk architecture supports this?
choices: A single web server tier environment with background threads
A web server environment and a separate worker environment, each in the same Elastic Beanstalk application
A multi-container Docker web server environment with web and worker containers
A web server environment with a DaemonSet sidecar for background processing
explanation_html:
Correct answer: A web server environment and a separate worker environment, each in the same Elastic Beanstalk application

Elastic Beanstalk supports two environment tiers: web server (handles HTTP requests) and worker (processes SQS messages via a daemon process). Separating them allows independent scaling — the worker scales based on SQS queue depth while the web tier scales based on HTTP traffic. The worker tier automatically manages the SQS queue integration (the sqsd daemon polls SQS and sends messages to the application's HTTP endpoint). Background threads in a single environment cannot scale independently. Multi-container Docker is a deployment platform, not an independent scaling architecture for workers.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features-managing-env-tiers.html

question: A developer wants to implement feature flags in their application hosted on AWS. Different users should see different features without redeploying the application. Which AWS service is best suited for this?
choices: AWS AppConfig with a feature flag configuration profile
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with a parameter per feature
AWS Secrets Manager with feature flag values
Amazon DynamoDB with a feature flag table
explanation_html:
Correct answer: AWS AppConfig with a feature flag configuration profile

AWS AppConfig is purpose-built for application configuration management and feature flags. It supports feature flag configuration profiles with a visual editor in the console, deployment strategies (immediate, linear, canary rollouts), validation, and the ability to quickly roll back if issues are detected. AppConfig can integrate with Lambda extensions for zero-latency config retrieval. SSM Parameter Store can store feature flags but lacks built-in deployment strategies, validation, and rollback. Secrets Manager is for sensitive credentials. DynamoDB is a database that can store feature flags but requires custom querying and has no built-in deployment management.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/appconfig-creating-feature-flags.html

question: A developer created a Lambda function that is triggered by an SNS topic. After deployment, the Lambda function is never invoked when messages are published to SNS. The SNS subscription shows as confirmed. What is the most likely missing configuration?
choices: The Lambda function is not in the same region as the SNS topic
The Lambda function's resource-based policy does not grant SNS permission to invoke it
The Lambda function's execution role does not have sns:Subscribe permission
SNS requires Lambda functions to be deployed in a VPC to invoke them
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The Lambda function's resource-based policy does not grant SNS permission to invoke it

For SNS to invoke a Lambda function, the Lambda function must have a resource-based policy that grants sns:Invoke (or lambda:InvokeFunction) permission to the SNS topic's ARN. Without this policy, SNS cannot call the Lambda function even if the subscription is confirmed. AWS CLI and console typically add this permission automatically when you create the SNS subscription, but manual configurations may miss it. The execution role controls what the Lambda function can do, not what can invoke it. Lambda functions do not need to be in a VPC for SNS invocations. Cross-region Lambda invocation from SNS is not supported.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sns.html

question: A developer needs to configure API Gateway to pass the original client IP address to a backend Lambda function. The function uses the IP for rate limiting and fraud detection. How is this configured in a Lambda proxy integration?
choices: Configure API Gateway to add a custom X-Forwarded-For header to the request
The client IP is automatically available in the event.requestContext.identity.sourceIp field in Lambda proxy integration
Configure a mapping template to extract the IP from the request context
Use API Gateway private integration to pass the client IP directly
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The client IP is automatically available in the event.requestContext.identity.sourceIp field in Lambda proxy integration

With Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway passes the full request context to the Lambda function in a structured event object. The client's IP address is available at event.requestContext.identity.sourceIp. No additional configuration is needed. This is one of the benefits of proxy integration — the Lambda function receives all request metadata including headers, query strings, path parameters, and request context. Custom mapping templates are needed for non-proxy integrations. X-Forwarded-For headers are automatically forwarded by API Gateway but the sourceIp field is the more reliable source.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-lambda-proxy-integrations.html

question: A developer is implementing CI/CD with CodePipeline. After a successful deployment to staging, the pipeline must run integration tests using a Lambda function and only proceed to production if all tests pass. The Lambda function is triggered by the pipeline and must report results back. Which CodePipeline integration type supports this with the Lambda function signaling continuation?
choices: A CodeBuild action in a test stage that invokes the Lambda function
A Lambda action where the function calls PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult to signal completion
An Approval action that the Lambda function approves programmatically
A CodeDeploy action with a Lambda lifecycle hook for testing
explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Lambda action where the function calls PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult to signal completion

CodePipeline's Lambda action type invokes a Lambda function and waits for the function to signal completion. The function receives a job ID and must call PutJobSuccessResult (to advance the pipeline) or PutJobFailureResult (to fail the pipeline) using the CodePipeline SDK. This decoupling allows the Lambda to perform asynchronous work before signaling. CodeBuild actions run build containers but require the test output in the buildspec. Approval actions require a human (or manual API call) to approve, not automatic Lambda signaling. CodeDeploy lifecycle hooks are for deployment events, not pipeline stage logic.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/actions-invoke-lambda-function.html

question: A developer is using the AWS SDK for JavaScript in a Lambda function. The function makes multiple independent DynamoDB GetItem calls and needs to minimize total execution time. What is the best approach?
choices: Make each GetItem call sequentially using await
Use DynamoDB BatchGetItem to retrieve all items in a single API call
Use Promise.all() to execute all GetItem calls concurrently
Use DynamoDB TransactGetItems for concurrent reads
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use DynamoDB BatchGetItem to retrieve all items in a single API call

BatchGetItem allows retrieving up to 100 items from one or more DynamoDB tables in a single API request. This reduces the number of network round trips compared to multiple individual GetItem calls. While Promise.all() makes concurrent calls, it still results in N separate API calls and N separate network connections. BatchGetItem is a single request/response cycle. Sequential awaits are the slowest option. TransactGetItems provides read consistency guarantees across items (like a transaction) but has higher overhead and is for cases requiring consistent multi-item reads, not just parallelism.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/WorkingWithItems.html

question: A developer is troubleshooting a Lambda function that intermittently fails with a 'connection pool is full' error when connecting to an RDS PostgreSQL database. The function scales to hundreds of concurrent invocations. What is the recommended solution?
choices: Increase the RDS instance max_connections parameter
Use Amazon RDS Proxy to pool and reuse database connections across Lambda invocations
Open and close the database connection inside the Lambda handler function
Switch to DynamoDB to avoid connection pool issues
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use Amazon RDS Proxy to pool and reuse database connections across Lambda invocations

Amazon RDS Proxy maintains a pool of connections to the database and multiplexes Lambda function connections through the pool. Hundreds of Lambda invocations can share a smaller pool of actual database connections, preventing the 'too many connections' problem. Each Lambda invocation connects to RDS Proxy (which is efficient), and RDS Proxy manages the real database connections. Increasing max_connections helps but has limits. Opening/closing connections in the handler is actually worse — Lambda best practice is to initialize connections outside the handler to reuse them across invocations. Switching databases is an architectural change that doesn't solve the underlying pattern.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html

question: A developer wants to use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy an IAM role to all accounts in an AWS Organization. The StackSet should automatically deploy to new accounts added to the organization. Which feature enables automatic deployment to new accounts?
choices: CloudFormation drift detection on the StackSet
Automatic deployment with organizational unit (OU) targeting and Automatic Deployment enabled
A CloudWatch Events rule that triggers a StackSet update when new accounts join
AWS Control Tower account factory integration with CloudFormation
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Automatic deployment with organizational unit (OU) targeting and Automatic Deployment enabled

CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions support targeting entire OUs. When you enable Automatic Deployment on the StackSet deployment options, CloudFormation automatically creates stack instances in new accounts added to the targeted OU and removes stack instances from accounts removed from the OU. This eliminates manual StackSet management for organizational changes. Drift detection identifies configuration differences. A CloudWatch Events rule requires custom Lambda logic. Control Tower can provision accounts but StackSet Automatic Deployment handles the deployment natively.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacksets-orgs-manage-auto-deployment.html

question: A developer is using Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a Node.js application. The application must read environment-specific configuration (database URL, feature flags) at startup. The values differ between staging and production environments. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Hardcode values in the application code with environment-specific if statements
Use Elastic Beanstalk environment properties to inject configuration as environment variables
Read configuration from a config file bundled in the deployment package
Use AWS AppConfig triggered by an Elastic Beanstalk lifecycle hook
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use Elastic Beanstalk environment properties to inject configuration as environment variables

Elastic Beanstalk environment properties are key-value pairs configured per environment that are injected as environment variables into the application's process. This allows the same deployment package to run in different environments with different configurations. Node.js applications read them via process.env. This is the standard Elastic Beanstalk configuration pattern. Hardcoding creates environment-specific code branches, which is an anti-pattern. Bundled config files require separate packages per environment. AppConfig is more appropriate for runtime feature flag changes, not initial environment configuration.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/environments-cfg-softwaresettings.html

question: A developer needs to implement a DynamoDB table that stores IoT sensor readings. Each sensor generates one reading per minute. Queries will filter by sensorId and a time range of the last hour. Scans should be avoided. What is the optimal table design?
choices: Partition key: sensorId, Sort key: timestamp — query with begins_with on timestamp
Partition key: sensorId, Sort key: timestamp — query with KeyConditionExpression using BETWEEN on timestamp
Partition key: timestamp, Sort key: sensorId — efficient time-range queries across all sensors
Partition key: sensorId only — use FilterExpression on timestamp
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Partition key: sensorId, Sort key: timestamp — query with KeyConditionExpression using BETWEEN on timestamp

Using sensorId as the partition key and timestamp as the sort key allows efficient queries by sensorId with a time range condition. The Query API supports KeyConditionExpression with BETWEEN, >=, <=, begins_with on the sort key. This retrieves only the relevant items without a scan. begins_with on timestamp would only work for string prefix matching. Using timestamp as partition key would scatter reads across partitions. FilterExpression with only a partition key still requires reading all items for that sensorId and then filtering in memory — it does not avoid reading unnecessary items.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Query.html

question: A developer is implementing API Gateway with a Lambda authorizer. The authorizer validates a JWT and returns an IAM policy. API Gateway caches the authorizer result. Cached authorization must be invalidated when a user's permissions change. What is the most effective approach?
choices: Set the authorizer's TTL to 0 to disable caching
Use a unique cache key that includes the user's role or permission hash
Manually flush the API Gateway authorizer cache from the console or API
Switch to a Cognito authorizer which doesn't cache permissions
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Manually flush the API Gateway authorizer cache from the console or API

API Gateway Lambda authorizer caches the IAM policy returned for a given token (or header/query string) for the configured TTL. When permissions change, you can flush the cache by calling the FlushStageAuthorizersCache API action or from the console. Alternatively, setting TTL to 0 disables caching but removes performance benefits. A unique cache key based on permissions hash is complex to implement and requires changing the token. Cognito authorizers also cache results. For permission changes, either accept the TTL delay, flush the cache programmatically, or set a short TTL based on your requirements.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/configure-api-gateway-lambda-authorization-with-console.html

question: A developer must ensure that all objects uploaded to an S3 bucket are encrypted with KMS. Unencrypted PUT requests should be automatically rejected. How is this enforced?
choices: Enable S3 default encryption with a KMS key — unencrypted objects are rejected
Add a bucket policy with a Deny condition for PutObject requests missing the x-amz-server-side-encryption header
Configure AWS Config to detect and delete unencrypted objects
Enable S3 Object Lock to require encryption on all objects
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Add a bucket policy with a Deny condition for PutObject requests missing the x-amz-server-side-encryption header

A bucket policy with a Deny statement and a null condition on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption rejects PutObject requests that don't specify encryption. Example: Deny s3:PutObject when aws:RequestedRegion is not null and s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is null, OR when the encryption header is not aws:kms. S3 default encryption applies encryption automatically to unencrypted uploads instead of rejecting them — it does not enforce KMS specifically or reject requests. AWS Config detects but doesn't prevent. S3 Object Lock is for WORM compliance, not encryption enforcement.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html

question: A developer needs to debug a Lambda function that is failing in production. The function runs 10,000 times per day. The developer needs to see the full execution logs including timing for specific slow invocations. How should logs be analyzed efficiently without manually searching through all invocations?
choices: Download all CloudWatch Logs and grep locally
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the log group and filter by duration or error patterns
Enable X-Ray tracing to see timing for every invocation
Set up a CloudWatch dashboard with Lambda duration metrics
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the log group and filter by duration or error patterns

CloudWatch Logs Insights can query millions of log entries in seconds. For Lambda, you can filter invocations by REPORT lines (which contain duration, billed duration, memory used) using queries like: filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@duration) by @requestId | sort @duration desc | limit 20. This efficiently identifies slow invocations without downloading or manually searching logs. Downloading logs locally is slow and impractical at scale. X-Ray traces every request (with sampling) but the Logs Insights query approach directly targets the log data. CloudWatch dashboards show aggregate metrics, not individual invocation logs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData.html

question: A developer is implementing AWS WAF on an API Gateway stage to block SQL injection attacks. WAF is configured but still allowing some SQL injection payloads. What is the most likely issue?
choices: WAF cannot be attached to API Gateway, only to CloudFront
The WAF web ACL is using a count action instead of a block action for the SQL injection rule
The WAF rules require Lambda@Edge to inspect request bodies
API Gateway must be deployed to a new stage for WAF rules to take effect
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The WAF web ACL is using a count action instead of a block action for the SQL injection rule

AWS WAF supports two actions for matching rules: Block (immediately returns a 403) and Count (logs the match but allows the request). A common misconfiguration is using Count for testing purposes and forgetting to switch to Block in production. WAF can be attached to API Gateway regional endpoints, CloudFront, ALB, and AppSync — the premise of option A is incorrect. WAF inspects request bodies natively without Lambda@Edge for regional APIs. WAF rules take effect immediately on associated resources; redeployment is not required.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/web-acl-rule-group-settings.html

question: A developer is building an application that needs to read configuration values from SSM Parameter Store without any latency overhead on each request. The values rarely change (updated once per week). What approach minimizes latency while staying current?
choices: Read the parameter on every request using GetParameter
Cache the parameter value in the Lambda global scope and refresh it on a scheduled basis using a separate Lambda
Use the AWS AppConfig Lambda extension which polls for updates and serves cached values locally
Store the parameter value in a DynamoDB table for faster access
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use the AWS AppConfig Lambda extension which polls for updates and serves cached values locally

The AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension (a Lambda layer) runs as a sidecar process and caches parameter values locally. The Lambda function retrieves values via a local HTTP call (localhost:2773) with zero network latency to SSM. The extension polls SSM in the background at a configurable interval to stay current. This eliminates SSM API calls on the hot path. Reading on every request adds SSM API latency and costs. Lambda global scope caching requires managing a separate refresh Lambda. DynamoDB would require provisioning infrastructure for a configuration cache use case.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/ps-integration-lambda-extensions.html

question: A developer receives a CloudWatch alarm indicating that a Lambda function's error rate has spiked to 30%. The function processes orders from SQS. What is the first step to diagnose the root cause?
choices: Increase the Lambda function memory and redeploy
Check CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function's log group to find error messages and stack traces
Increase the SQS visibility timeout to give Lambda more time
Add more Lambda concurrency to process messages faster
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Check CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function's log group to find error messages and stack traces

The first step in diagnosing Lambda errors is checking CloudWatch Logs, which contains the function's stdout, stderr, and AWS-generated START, END, and REPORT log lines. Error messages and stack traces in the logs identify the exact exception type, the line of code that failed, and the context (input event) at the time of failure. Without understanding the error, any other change (memory, timeout, concurrency) would be guesswork. Lambda automatically streams all function output to CloudWatch Logs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/monitoring-cloudwatchlogs.html

question: A developer is writing a CloudFormation template and needs to construct a string that combines a static prefix with a parameter value and a resource attribute. For example: 'arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket-' + AccountId + '-' + BucketName. Which CloudFormation function should be used?
choices: Fn::Join with a list of values
Fn::Sub with a substitution string
Fn::Select with an index
Fn::If with a conditional expression
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Fn::Sub with a substitution string

Fn::Sub substitutes variables (${VariableName}) in a string with their values from parameters, resources, or pseudo-parameters like AWS::AccountId. Example: 'arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket-${AWS::AccountId}-${BucketName}'. This is more readable than Fn::Join for complex string construction. Fn::Join concatenates an array of values with a delimiter — achievable but less readable for complex interpolations. Fn::Select picks one value from a list by index. Fn::If returns one of two values based on a condition.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/intrinsic-function-reference-sub.html

question: A developer deploys an ECS service using the Fargate launch type. The task needs 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM. Which ECS task definition CPU and memory combination is valid for Fargate?
choices: CPU: 4096, Memory: 8192
CPU: 4, Memory: 8
CPU: 4000, Memory: 8000
CPU: 4 vCPU, Memory: 8 GB (selected from a dropdown)
explanation_html:
Correct answer: CPU: 4096, Memory: 8192

Fargate uses CPU units (1 vCPU = 1024 CPU units) and memory in MiB. To request 4 vCPUs, specify 4096 CPU units. For 8 GB RAM, specify 8192 MiB. Fargate has specific valid CPU/memory combinations: 4096 CPU supports 8192–30720 MiB memory in 1024 MiB increments. Using plain integers like 4 or 8 is invalid for the API values. The 'vCPU' and 'GB' notations are used in the console for readability but the underlying API values are CPU units and MiB respectively.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-cpu-memory-error.html

question: A developer uses X-Ray to trace a Lambda function that calls DynamoDB and an external payment API. The trace shows the Lambda segment and the DynamoDB subsegment, but the payment API call is missing. What must the developer add to capture the payment API subsegment?
choices: Enable X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda function
Instrument the HTTP client with the X-Ray SDK (e.g., AWSXRay.captureHTTPs or AWSXRay.captureAsyncFunc)
Add the X-Ray SDK as a Lambda layer
Call AWSXRay.beginSegment('payment-api') before the HTTP call
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Instrument the HTTP client with the X-Ray SDK (e.g., AWSXRay.captureHTTPs or AWSXRay.captureAsyncFunc)

X-Ray automatically captures AWS SDK calls (including DynamoDB) when the AWS SDK is patched via AWSXRay.captureAWS(AWS). However, calls to external HTTP endpoints (like a payment API) require explicit instrumentation. In Node.js, use AWSXRay.captureHTTPs(require('https')) to patch the built-in https module so all outgoing requests create subsegments. Active tracing enables the Lambda-X-Ray integration but does not auto-capture external HTTP. The X-Ray daemon is embedded in Lambda. AWSXRay.beginSegment would create a new root segment, not a subsegment of the existing Lambda segment.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-sdk-nodejs-httpclients.html

question: A developer runs a CloudWatch Logs Insights query and wants to visualize the results as a time series chart in a CloudWatch dashboard. The query aggregates error counts by 5-minute intervals. What must the query use to produce time series data?
choices: The filter command with a time range parameter
The stats command with count() grouped by bin(@timestamp, 5m)
The sort command by @timestamp
The fields command to select @timestamp and @message
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The stats command with count() grouped by bin(@timestamp, 5m)

To produce time series data in Logs Insights, use the stats command with an aggregation function (count, sum, avg, etc.) grouped by bin(@timestamp, period). The bin() function rounds timestamps to the specified interval, creating data points for each time bucket. This produces tabular output that CloudWatch can render as a time series visualization. The filter command selects log events but doesn't aggregate. The sort command orders results. The fields command selects specific fields but doesn't aggregate into time buckets.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CWL_QuerySyntax.html

question: A developer needs to optimize a Lambda function's performance. The function initializes a large ML model (500 MB) on every cold start, adding 8 seconds of initialization time. The function processes real-time requests that must respond in under 1 second. What is the most effective architectural change?
choices: Store the model in S3 and download it on every invocation
Use Lambda SnapStart to snapshot the initialized execution environment with the model loaded
Load the model in the Lambda handler function to avoid initialization overhead
Increase the Lambda function memory to the maximum to speed up model loading
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use Lambda SnapStart to snapshot the initialized execution environment with the model loaded

Lambda SnapStart (for Java runtimes) takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment after the init phase completes. Subsequent invocations restore from the snapshot, eliminating the initialization time. For the ML model use case, the model is loaded during init, snapshotted, and subsequent cold starts restore the pre-loaded model state instantly. For non-Java runtimes, provisioned concurrency achieves a similar effect by keeping initialized environments warm. Downloading the model on every invocation increases latency. Loading in the handler (not global scope) means loading on every invocation. Memory increases can speed up loading but cannot eliminate 8 seconds of work.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/snapstart.html

question: A developer wants to test a Lambda function with a simulated Kinesis Data Streams event locally before deploying. Which SAM CLI command generates a sample event payload for testing?
choices: sam local invoke --event kinesis
sam generate-event kinesis get-records
sam local generate-event --source kinesis
sam event create --type kinesis
explanation_html:
Correct answer: sam generate-event kinesis get-records

The SAM CLI sam generate-event command generates sample event payloads for various AWS services. For Kinesis: sam generate-event kinesis get-records outputs a JSON payload matching the event structure that Lambda receives from Kinesis Data Streams. This can be piped to sam local invoke: sam generate-event kinesis get-records | sam local invoke MyFunction. The other options use incorrect command syntax that does not exist in the SAM CLI.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/serverless-application-model/latest/developerguide/sam-cli-command-reference-sam-local-generate-event.html

question: A developer is using CodeDeploy to deploy to EC2 instances. The deployment fails with 'The deployment failed because no instances were found in your deployment group'. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The EC2 instances do not have the CodeDeploy agent installed and running
The CodeDeploy service role does not have EC2 permissions
The deployment group's tag filters do not match any EC2 instances
The appspec.yml is missing from the deployment bundle
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The deployment group's tag filters do not match any EC2 instances

The error 'no instances were found in your deployment group' specifically indicates that CodeDeploy cannot find EC2 instances matching the deployment group's tag or Auto Scaling group configuration. CodeDeploy identifies target instances by EC2 tags or Auto Scaling group membership. If the tags specified in the deployment group (e.g., Environment: Production) don't match any instances, no instances are found. Missing CodeDeploy agent would result in a different error (agent not responding). Missing service role permissions would fail at a different point. Missing appspec.yml would fail after instances are found.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-deployments.html

question: A developer is designing a Lambda function to process user uploads. The function must validate the file type, resize images, and store the result in S3. The developer notices the function takes 30 seconds for large images. The function timeout is 15 minutes. What change most reduces function duration?
choices: Increase Lambda memory — more memory means more CPU proportionally
Use a separate Lambda function for each step and chain them with Step Functions
Move image resizing to EC2 Spot Instances for cheaper compute
Use Lambda response streaming to return partial results faster
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Increase Lambda memory — more memory means more CPU proportionally

Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to the configured memory. At 128 MB (minimum), a function receives a fraction of a vCPU. At 1769 MB, a function receives one full vCPU. Above 1769 MB, the function receives more than one vCPU (up to 6 vCPUs at 10240 MB). For CPU-intensive tasks like image processing, increasing memory directly increases processing speed, often reducing duration enough to lower cost despite higher memory cost. Step Functions adds orchestration overhead for a single function. EC2 Spot Instances require significant infrastructure management. Response streaming returns results incrementally but doesn't speed up actual processing.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/operatorguide/perf-optimize.html

question: A developer configured CloudWatch Container Insights on an ECS cluster. They want to see memory utilization per ECS service in a single CloudWatch dashboard widget. Which metric should they use?
choices: AWS/ECS MemoryUtilization dimension: ClusterName
ECS/ContainerInsights MemoryUtilized dimension: ClusterName, ServiceName
AWS/EC2 mem_used_percent dimension: InstanceId
AWS/ECS ContainerMemoryUsed dimension: ServiceName
explanation_html:
Correct answer: ECS/ContainerInsights MemoryUtilized dimension: ClusterName, ServiceName

CloudWatch Container Insights publishes enhanced metrics to the ECS/ContainerInsights namespace (not AWS/ECS). These metrics include MemoryUtilized and MemoryReserved at the cluster, service, task, and container level. To see per-service memory utilization, use the ECS/ContainerInsights namespace with MemoryUtilized or MemoryUtilization dimensions including ClusterName and ServiceName. AWS/ECS contains only basic metrics (CPUUtilization, MemoryUtilization at the service level). EC2 metrics are for the underlying instances. There is no ContainerMemoryUsed metric in AWS/ECS.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Container-Insights-metrics-ECS.html

question: A developer wants to ensure that multiple Lambda functions in the same account share the same codebase but can have different environment configurations (dev, staging, prod). Which Lambda feature enables managing different configurations per environment without separate function deployments?
