choices: Lambda layers for shared code with separate functions per environment
Lambda function aliases pointing to the same version with different environment variable configurations per alias
Lambda versions with different environment variables per version
A single Lambda function with if/else logic checking the ENVIRONMENT variable
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Lambda function aliases pointing to the same version with different environment variable configurations per alias

Lambda aliases can have their own environment variable configurations that override the function's default environment variables. You publish one function version (immutable code) and create multiple aliases (dev, staging, prod) each pointing to the same version but with different environment variables (database URLs, feature flags, etc.). This allows one codebase to serve multiple environments with isolated configurations. Layers share code but don't manage environment configuration. Lambda versions are immutable including their environment variables — you can't change them per environment. Hardcoded if/else logic couples configuration to code.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-aliases.html

question: A developer is implementing a serverless API. The API must handle both authenticated requests (using Cognito) and unauthenticated requests (public endpoints). How should the developer configure API Gateway to support both?
choices: Create two separate API Gateway APIs, one with a Cognito authorizer and one without
Configure the Cognito authorizer on the specific routes that require authentication; leave public routes with no authorizer
Use a Lambda authorizer that allows both authenticated and unauthenticated requests
Configure API Gateway with an API key for public routes and Cognito for authenticated routes
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure the Cognito authorizer on the specific routes that require authentication; leave public routes with no authorizer

API Gateway allows configuring authorization at the route/method level. You can apply a Cognito User Pool authorizer to specific routes (e.g., POST /orders, GET /profile) that require authentication while leaving other routes (e.g., GET /products, GET /health) with NONE authorization. This is the standard pattern for mixed-auth APIs. Two separate APIs add unnecessary complexity and duplication. A Lambda authorizer could allow both but adds extra invocation overhead. API keys are for usage tracking/throttling, not authentication.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-integrate-with-cognito.html

question: A developer is setting up CodePipeline to deploy a serverless SAM application. After the CodeBuild stage produces a packaged SAM template, which CodePipeline action type should be used to execute the CloudFormation change set and deploy the stack?
choices: AWS CodeDeploy — deploy the packaged SAM template
AWS CloudFormation — create or replace a change set, then execute the change set
AWS Lambda — invoke a Lambda function to run sam deploy
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — deploy the application bundle
explanation_html:
Correct answer: AWS CloudFormation — create or replace a change set, then execute the change set

SAM templates are CloudFormation templates with a transform. CodePipeline's CloudFormation action type can create and execute change sets directly. The standard SAM deployment pipeline uses: (1) CodeBuild: sam build && sam package (uploads artifacts to S3, produces packaged template). (2) CodePipeline CloudFormation action: CREATE_UPDATE or CHANGE_SET_CREATE then CHANGE_SET_EXECUTE. CodeDeploy is for EC2/Lambda/ECS deployments, not SAM template deployments. Invoking sam deploy via Lambda is a workaround, not the native approach. Elastic Beanstalk deploys web applications, not serverless stacks.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/action-reference-CloudFormation.html

question: A developer must ensure a Lambda function only processes each SQS message exactly once, even if SQS delivers the message multiple times. The function writes the processed result to DynamoDB. What is the most reliable way to achieve exactly-once semantics?
choices: Use an SQS FIFO queue which guarantees exactly-once processing
Check if the message ID has already been processed in DynamoDB before processing; skip if found
Set the SQS visibility timeout to 24 hours to prevent re-delivery
Use Lambda reserved concurrency of 1 to prevent concurrent processing
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Check if the message ID has already been processed in DynamoDB before processing; skip if found

Implementing idempotency is the correct approach for exactly-once semantics. Before processing, check a DynamoDB deduplication table for the SQS message ID. If found, skip processing (already done). If not found, write the message ID and process it atomically (using DynamoDB conditional writes). SQS FIFO guarantees exactly-once delivery during a 5-minute deduplication window, but Lambda processing can still fail mid-execution causing retry — the function still needs to be idempotent. A 24-hour visibility timeout prevents re-delivery during processing but not after a function crash. Concurrency of 1 serializes processing but does not prevent duplicate processing on retry.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-idempotence.html
